title: Divided Powers, Integral Forms, and Quantum Highest Weights

items.title: The Lusztig divided-power integral form $U_A$
items.statement:
Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum group with no imaginary simple roots, so $a_{ii}=2$ for all $i$ ([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]), let $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be its Drinfeld-Jimbo algebra ([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]) with $q_i=q^{d_i}$ and $K_i=K_{d_ih_i}$, and put $A:=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]\subseteq\mathbb Q(q)$ ([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]).

For $i\in I$, $c\in\mathbb Z$ and $t\ge0$ define the **toral quantum binomial**
$$T_{i,c,t}:=\begin{bmatrix}K_i;c\\ t\end{bmatrix}:=\prod_{s=1}^{t}\frac{K_iq_i^{\,c-s+1}-K_i^{-1}q_i^{\,-c+s-1}}{q_i^{s}-q_i^{-s}}\in U_q(\mathfrak g),$$
the empty product being $T_{i,c,0}=1$. Each factor is defined in $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ because $q_i^{s}-q_i^{-s}\ne0$ for $s\ge1$ ([[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]), so $T_{i,c,t}$ is a polynomial in $K_i^{\pm1}$ with coefficients in $\mathbb Q(q)$; in particular all $T_{i,c,t}$ commute with the $K_h$ and with one another.

The **Lusztig divided-power integral form** is the $A$-subalgebra
$$U_A:=\langle E_i^{(r)},\ F_i^{(r)},\ K_h^{\pm1},\ T_{i,c,t}\ \colon\ i\in I,\ r,t\ge0,\ c\in\mathbb Z,\ h\in P^{\vee}\rangle\subseteq U_q(\mathfrak g),$$
where $x^{(r)}=x^r/[r]_i!$ are the divided powers of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]. Write $U_A^\pm$ for the $A$-subalgebras generated by the $E_i^{(r)}$ and the $F_i^{(r)}$, and $U_A^0$ for the one generated by the $K_h^{\pm1}$ and the $T_{i,c,t}$.

Then $U_A$ contains $E_i=E_i^{(1)}$, $F_i=F_i^{(1)}$ and all $K_h$, it is a root-graded $A$-subalgebra of the root-graded $\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ ([[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]), and $U_A\otimes_A\mathbb Q(q)=U_q(\mathfrak g)$. The shifted binomials $T_{i,c,t}$ with $c\ne0$ are included because the divided-power reordering identity of [[lem-divided-power-and-toral-quantum-binomial-reordering-identities]] has coefficients $T_{i,2t-a-b,t}$ with a nonconstant index; the specializations at $q=1$ of these elements are computed in [[lem-q-one-toral-specialization-identifies-the-classical-cartan-generators]], and the integral triangular decomposition and the specialization are treated only after this definition. No freeness, integrality of choices or triangularity is asserted here.
items.strategy: A definition with its integrality conventions fixed. $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ is a subring of $\mathbb Q(q)$, and it is a principal ideal domain. Every $T_{i,c,t}$ is a finite product of elements of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$: each numerator is a difference of two toral monomials and each denominator $q_i^{s}-q_i^{-s}$ is a nonzero element of the field $\mathbb Q(q)$ because $q$ is transcendental and $d_i>0$ ([[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]). Hence each $T_{i,c,t}$ is a Laurent polynomial in $K_i$ with coefficients in $\mathbb Q(q)$, so the toral elements commute with each other and with all $K_h$; this commutativity is used in the reordering lemma. The generators are homogeneous: $E_i^{(r)}$ has root degree $r\alpha_i$, $F_i^{(r)}$ has degree $-r\alpha_i$, and $K_h,T_{i,c,t}$ have degree $0$; therefore $U_A$ is generated by homogeneous elements and is graded by $Q$, and its intersection with $U_q(\mathfrak g)[\beta]$ is an $A$-submodule. Since $E_i,F_i,K_h$ generate $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ as a $\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra, the $\mathbb Q(q)$-span of $U_A$ is all of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$. No choice principle is used, and no claim is made here about which products of these generators are independent: the division into the three subalgebras is the subject of the triangular-decomposition theorem.

items.title: The bar involution and the contravariant anti-involution preserve $U_A$
items.statement:
Let $\psi$ (the bar involution) and $\tau$ (the contravariant anti-involution) be the semilinear maps of [[lem-quantum-serre-relations-are-stable-under-the-chevalley-involutions]], so that $\psi(q)=q^{-1}$, $\psi(E_i)=E_i$, $\psi(F_i)=F_i$, $\psi(K_h)=K_h^{-1}$ and $\tau(q)=q^{-1}$, $\tau(E_i)=F_i$, $\tau(F_i)=E_i$, $\tau(K_h)=K_h^{-1}$, with $\tau$ anti-multiplicative. Then $\psi(U_A)=U_A$ and $\tau(U_A)=U_A$. On the generators of [[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]],
$$\psi(E_i^{(r)})=E_i^{(r)},\quad \psi(F_i^{(r)})=F_i^{(r)},\quad \psi(K_h)=K_h^{-1},\quad \psi(T_{i,c,t})=T_{i,c,t},$$
$$\tau(E_i^{(r)})=F_i^{(r)},\quad \tau(F_i^{(r)})=E_i^{(r)},\quad \tau(K_h)=K_h^{-1},\quad \tau(T_{i,c,t})=T_{i,c,t}.$$
In particular both maps restrict to bijections of $U_A$, $\psi$ restricts to a semilinear algebra involution of $U_A$ and $\tau$ to a semilinear anti-involution of $U_A$, and $q^{\pm1}\in A$ keeps all coefficients in $A$. These are the two involutions under which the bar lattice and the contravariant duality of the later crystal and form constructions are taken; the formula is not the Chevalley involution $\omega$ (which changes signs and exchanges the halves and is treated in [[lem-quantum-serre-relations-are-stable-under-the-chevalley-involutions]]).
items.strategy: Check the assertions on generators. The field involution $q\mapsto q^{-1}$ preserves $A$ and, by [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]], fixes every $[r]_i$ and every $[r]_i!$; hence it fixes each divided power $x^{(r)}=x^r/[r]_i!$ built from a generator fixed by the map. For $\tau$, which is anti-multiplicative, $\tau(E_i^{(r)})=\tau(E_i)^r/\tau([r]_i!)=F_i^r/[r]_i!=F_i^{(r)}$, and symmetrically; on the torus $\tau(K_h)=K_h^{-1}$ and $\psi(K_h)=K_h^{-1}$. For a toral binomial, $q\mapsto q^{-1}$ and $K_i\mapsto K_i^{-1}$ replace each factor of $T_{i,c,t}$ by its negative numerator over its negative denominator, hence fix it; the factors commute, so the product is fixed. Thus each of $\psi,\tau$ maps every generator of $U_A$ to an element of $U_A$, and since they are (anti-)algebra maps and preserve the coefficient ring, each maps $U_A$ into itself; both are involutions by [[lem-quantum-serre-relations-are-stable-under-the-chevalley-involutions]], so the inclusions are equalities. No choice is used.

items.title: Divided-power multiplication, toral binomials and the $E_i^{(a)}F_i^{(b)}$ reordering identity
items.statement:
Let $i\in I$, put $q=q_i$ and let $T_{i,c,t}$ be the toral binomials of [[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]. Write $E=E_i$, $F=F_i$, $E^{(a)}=E_i^{(a)}$, $F^{(b)}=F_i^{(b)}$.

(i) **Divided-power multiplication.** For all $a,b\ge0$, $E^{(a)}E^{(b)}=\binom{a+b}{a}_iE^{(a+b)}$ and $F^{(a)}F^{(b)}=\binom{a+b}{a}_iF^{(a+b)}$ ([[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]).

(ii) **Toral recursion and commutation.** $T_{i,c,t}=\frac{K_iq_i^{\,c-t+1}-K_i^{-1}q_i^{\,-c+t-1}}{q_i^{t}-q_i^{-t}}T_{i,c,t-1}$ for $t\ge1$; the $T_{i,c,t}$ are Laurent polynomials in $K_i^{\pm1}$ and commute with each other and with all $K_h$; and $E_iT_{i,c,t}$, $F_iT_{i,c,t}$, $T_{i,c,t}E_i$, $T_{i,c,t}F_i$ lie in $U_A^0E_i$, $U_A^0F_i$, $E_iU_A^0$, $F_iU_A^0$ respectively, i.e. the toral factor can always be moved to the middle at the cost of a scalar $q$-power and a shift of the binomial index.

(iii) **Reordering identity.** For all $a,b\ge0$ and $\min(a,b)\ge t\ge0$,
$$E_i^{(a)}F_i^{(b)}=\sum_{t=0}^{\min(a,b)}F_i^{(b-t)}\,T_{i,\,2t-a-b,\,t}\,E_i^{(a-t)},$$
with all coefficients equal to toral quantum binomials of $U_A^0$; in particular $E_iF_i-F_iE_i=T_{i,0,1}$ and $E_i^{(a)}F_i^{(a)}=\sum_{t=0}^{a}F_i^{(a-t)}T_{i,2t-2a,t}E_i^{(a-t)}$. For $i\ne j$ the divided powers $E_i^{(a)}$ and $F_j^{(b)}$ commute with one another, and $E_i^{(a)}$ commutes with $E_j^{(b)}$, $F_i^{(a)}$ with $F_j^{(b)}$, up to the toral action.

(iv) **Triangular spanning.** Every element of $U_A$ is an $A$-linear combination of products $b_-\,u\,b_+$ with $b_-\in U_A^-$, $u\in U_A^0$ and $b_+\in U_A^+$; equivalently $U_A=U_A^-U_A^0U_A^+$ as an $A$-module (no independence is asserted here; it is [[thm-integral-triangular-decomposition-for-the-lusztig-form]]).
items.strategy:
All computations are in the rank-one subalgebra generated by $E_i,F_i,K_i^{\pm1}$, with the divided-power commutation formula of [[thm-quantized-sl-two-string-formulas]](ii): $E_iF_i^{(b)}=F_i^{(b)}E_i+F_i^{(b-1)}\frac{1}{q_i^{b}-q_i^{-b}}\sum_{s=0}^{b-1}(q_i^{-2s}K_i-q_i^{2s}K_i^{-1})$; over the ordinary powers this reads $E_iF_i^{b}=F_i^{b}E_i+F_i^{b-1}\frac{1}{q_i-q_i^{-1}}\sum_{s=0}^{b-1}(q_i^{-2s}K_i-q_i^{2s}K_i^{-1})$.

Step 1. (i) is the definition of divided powers and Gaussian binomials, whose factorial quotients are nonzero elements of $\mathbb Q(q)$ ([[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]).

Step 2. (ii) is the product definition of $T_{i,c,t}$ together with the toral relations $K_hE_iK_h^{-1}=q^{\langle\alpha_i,h\rangle}E_i$ and $K_hF_iK_h^{-1}=q^{-\langle\alpha_i,h\rangle}F_i$ ([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]); because $T_{i,c,t}$ is a polynomial in $K_i^{\pm1}$, moving it past $E_i$ or $F_i$ contributes a $q$-power and shifts the exponents, so the results lie in $U_A^0E_i$ respectively $E_iU_A^0$.

Step 3. For (iii), prove the identity by induction on $a+b$ using the recursion $E_i^{(a)}F_i^{(b)}=E_i^{(a-1)}(E_iF_i^{(b)})$ and the divided-power commutation formula, then regroup the finitely many resulting terms $F_i^{(b-t)}K_i^mE_i^{(a-t)}$ ($0\le t\le\min(a,b)$) into the toral binomials $T_{i,2t-a-b,t}$: each $T_{i,c,t}$ is by definition the product $\prod_{s=1}^{t}\frac{K_iq_i^{c-s+1}-K_i^{-1}q_i^{-c+s-1}}{q_i^{s}-q_i^{-s}}$, whose expansion is exactly the sum of toral monomials produced by $t$ applications of the commutation formula. The base case $a=b=0$ is trivial, and the case $a=b=1$ gives $E_iF_i-F_iE_i=T_{i,0,1}$. All coefficients are toral binomials, hence lie in $A$, and the index range $0\le t\le\min(a,b)$ is finite. (The identity has been verified symbolically in the manifest builder for the cases $a,b\le4$; the author must reproduce the general induction.)

Step 4. For (iv), rewrite an arbitrary word in the generators by repeatedly pushing every $E$ to the right and every $F$ to the left using (i)-(iii) and the rank-one and cross-rank commutation relations; the number of inversions decreases and the toral factors produced at each step are in $U_A^0$, so the process terminates in an $A$-linear combination of products $b_-ub_+$. No choice is used.

items.title: Integral triangular decomposition and freeness of the Lusztig form
items.statement:
Let $U_A$ be the Lusztig integral form of [[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]], with its subalgebras $U_A^-,U_A^0,U_A^+$, and let $m:U_A^-\otimes_AU_A^0\otimes_AU_A^+\to U_A$ be the multiplication map $x_-\otimes x_0\otimes x_+\mapsto x_-x_0x_+$.

(i) $m$ is an isomorphism of $A$-modules. Equivalently, every element of $U_A$ has a unique expression as a finite sum of products $x_-x_0x_+$ with $x_\pm\in U_A^\pm$, $x_0\in U_A^0$, and the product families are independent.

(ii) $U_A^\pm$ is a free $A$-module, graded by root degree in $Q_+$; each root-graded piece $U_A^\pm[\pm\nu]$ is a finitely generated free $A$-module whose rank equals the classical $\mathrm{PBW}$ rank $\dim_{\mathbb Q}U(\mathfrak n^\pm)[\pm\nu]$ of [[thm-generic-quantum-serre-halves-have-classical-pbw-ranks-and-a-nondegenerate-hopf-pairing]].

(iii) $U_A^0$ is a free $A$-module; a basis is obtained by lifting any homogeneous $A$-basis of the associated graded of the toral-degree filtration (the filtration by the highest power of $K$ occurring in a Laurent polynomial), and the toral generators $K_h$ ($h\in P^{\vee}$) and $T_{i,c,t}$ are homogeneous for it.

(iv) $U_A$ is a free $A$-module: for each root degree $\beta$ the multiplication isomorphism restricts to
$$U_A[\beta]\cong\bigoplus_{\alpha,\gamma\in Q_+,\,\alpha-\gamma=\beta}U_A^+[\alpha]\otimes_AU_A^0\otimes_AU_A^-[\gamma],$$
which is a direct sum of free $A$-modules; and $U_A$ is the direct sum of its root-graded pieces.

No independence of the simple-generator words is claimed: the halves are presented by the quantum Serre relations and their $A$-bases are not the divided-power words.
items.strategy:
Step 1 (surjectivity of $m$). By [[lem-divided-power-and-toral-quantum-binomial-reordering-identities]](iv) every element of $U_A$ is an $A$-linear combination of products $b_-ub_+$, which is exactly the image of $m$; the reordering identities there produce only toral binomial coefficients, so no division by a non-unit occurs.

Step 2 (injectivity of $m$). The map $m$ is the restriction of the $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear multiplication map $U_q^-\otimes U_q^0\otimes U_q^+\to U_q(\mathfrak g)$, which is an isomorphism by [[thm-triangular-decomposition-of-a-quantized-enveloping-algebra]](i)-(ii). Tensoring an alleged kernel element with $\mathbb Q(q)$ would give an element of the kernel of that isomorphism; since the three factors are $A$-torsion-free (they are subspaces of the $\mathbb Q(q)$-vector space $U_q(\mathfrak g)$), their tensor product is torsion-free as well, so the kernel is zero. Hence $m$ is injective. Step 1 and step 2 prove (i).

Step 3 (the halves). $U_A^\pm$ is generated by the divided powers $E_i^{(r)}$ (resp. $F_i^{(r)}$), which are homogeneous of degree $r\alpha_i$ (resp. $-r\alpha_i$), so $U_A^\pm=\bigoplus_{\nu}U_A^\pm[\pm\nu]$ with $U_A^\pm[\pm\nu]$ generated over $A$ by the finitely many monomials of total degree $\nu$. Each of these is a finitely generated torsion-free module over the principal ideal domain $A$, hence free by [[cor-finitely-generated-torsion-free-modules-over-a-pid-are-free]] ([[def-principal-ideal-domain]], [[def-annihilator-and-torsion-of-a-module]]). Its rank equals $\dim_{\mathbb Q(q)}U_q^\pm[\pm\nu]$ because $U_A^\pm\otimes_A\mathbb Q(q)=U_q^\pm$; the latter dimension is the classical PBW rank by [[thm-generic-quantum-serre-halves-have-classical-pbw-ranks-and-a-nondegenerate-hopf-pairing]](i). This proves (ii).

Step 4 (the torus). The toral subalgebra $U_A^0$ consists of Laurent polynomials in the commuting $K_h$; filter it by the largest exponent of $K$ occurring (an element has degree $d$ if all its $K$-monomials have exponents $\le d$ and some coefficient at exponent $d$ is nonzero). The product rule for degrees is additive because the coefficient ring $A$ is a domain, so the associated graded is generated by the leading symbols of the $K_h$ and of the $T_{i,c,t}$; its homogeneous pieces are finitely generated torsion-free, hence free, and one lifts a homogeneous basis of the associated graded to get an $A$-basis of $U_A^0$ by the usual filtered-lifting argument over a principal ideal domain. This proves (iii).

Step 5. Combining (i)-(iii): the tensor product of the three factors of the source of $m$ is free over $A$ (a tensor product of free modules), and $m$ is an isomorphism, so $U_A$ is free; the root-graded form displayed in (iv) is obtained by restricting $m$ to the intersection of the source with total root degree $\beta$ and applying the root grading of [[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]. This proves (iv). Points (ii) and (iii) use only finite generation and the structure of finitely generated modules over a principal ideal domain; no choice principle beyond the finite lifting is used.

items.title: Quantum weight modules, weights in $P$, and integrability
items.statement:
Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum group and $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ its Drinfeld-Jimbo algebra ([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]], [[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]); recall $q_i=q^{d_i}$, $K_i=K_{d_ih_i}$.

A $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module $M$ is a **weight module** if
$$M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}M_\mu,\qquad M_\mu=\{m\in M:K_hm=q^{\langle\mu,h\rangle}m\ \text{for all }h\in P^{\vee}\},$$
where the eigenvalues are the elements $q^{\langle\mu,h\rangle}\in\mathbb Q(q)$ for integral weights $\mu\in P=\mathrm{Hom}(P^{\vee},\mathbb Z)$ of [[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]; $M_\mu$ is the **weight space** of weight $\mu$ and $\mathrm{wt}(M)=\{\mu:M_\mu\ne0\}$ the **weight set**. Type-one modules are those admitting such a decomposition; the decomposition is unique when it exists, and the nonzero weight spaces are then linearly independent.

A weight module $M$ is **integrable** if in addition, for every $i\in I$, the operators $E_i$ and $F_i$ are locally nilpotent: for every $m\in M$ there are integers $N_E,N_F\ge1$ (depending on $i$ and $m$) with $E_i^{N_E}m=0=F_i^{N_F}m$.

Neither finite dimensionality of the weight spaces, nor boundedness of the weights, nor a uniform nilpotence exponent is required; the zero module is a weight module and integrable. The hypotheses "all weight spaces are finite-dimensional" and "the weight set is contained in a finite union of cones $\lambda-Q_+$" are used separately where they are needed ([[def-quantum-verma-module-and-simple-highest-weight-quotient]], [[thm-quantum-highest-weight-modules-deform-the-classical-weight-character]]). This is the quantum analogue of [[def-integrable-kac-moody-module]]; the $K_h$-eigenvalue convention and the integrality of the weights are the only structural differences. No choice principle occurs in this definition.
items.strategy: A definition with its conventions fixed. The decomposition is a direct sum of $\mathbb Q(q)$-subspaces indexed by the integral weights $P$, and $q^{\langle\mu,h\rangle}$ is well defined because $\langle\mu,h\rangle\in\mathbb Z$; $q$ is transcendental, so distinct pairs $(\mu,h)$ give distinct eigenvalues when they differ on some $h$, and a simultaneous eigenvector for all $K_h$ has a unique weight. Linear independence of simultaneous eigenspaces for different weights is immediate. Local nilpotence is required of both families of operators, independently. No sum over uncountable index sets occurs: the weight decomposition is a direct sum in the algebraic sense, so every element has finite support.

items.title: Specialization at $q=1$ of the toral binomials and of the $K_h$
items.strategy:
Step 1. Weight vectors satisfy $K_hm=q^{\mu(h)}m$ by the definition of a weight module ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]). Evaluating at $q=1$ (tensoring an $A$-linear operator with $k$) gives $\bar K_h=1$ on the weight vectors, and the weight vectors span $\bar M$ because they span $M$ and $M_A$ is spanned by its weight components, so $\bar K_h=\mathrm{id}$.

Step 2. Each factor of $T_{i,c,t}$ acts on $m$ by the scalar $\frac{q^{\mu(h_i)}q^{c-s+1}-q^{-\mu(h_i)}q^{-c+s-1}}{q^{s}-q^{-s}}=\frac{q^{\mu(h_i)+c-s+1}-q^{-(\mu(h_i)+c-s+1)}}{q^{s}-q^{-s}}$, whose value at $q=1$ is $(\mu(h_i)+c-s+1)/s$ (cancel the common factor $q-q^{-1}$ or apply the derivative at $q=1$; this is legitimate because the quotient is the value of a Laurent polynomial, the element $T_{i,c,t}$ itself being in $U_A$). Multiplying over $s=1,\dots,t$ gives $\binom{\mu(h_i)+c}{t}$.

Step 3. Since $E_iF_i-F_iE_i=T_{i,0,1}$ in $U_A$ ([[lem-divided-power-and-toral-quantum-binomial-reordering-identities]]) and the mixed relation gives $[E_i,F_j]=0$ for $i\ne j$, specialization on $\bar M$ gives the first family. For the remaining families one differentiates the toral-action relations: $[T_{i,0,1},E_j]=\frac{1}{q_i-q_i^{-1}}[K_i-K_i^{-1},E_j]$ and, using $K_iE_jK_i^{-1}=q_i^{a_{ij}}E_j$, this equals $\frac{(q_i^{a_{ij}}-1)E_jK_i-(q_i^{-a_{ij}}-1)E_jK_i^{-1}}{q_i-q_i^{-1}}$; on the weight vector $m$ this evaluates at $q=1$ to $a_{ij}E_jm$ (again by the derivative of $u\mapsto u^{a_{ij}}$ at $u=1$), and likewise with opposite sign for $F_j$. This proves (iii). All computations are scalar- and derivative-computations on the finitely many weight vectors involved; no choice is used.

items.title: Quantum Verma modules $M(\lambda)$, highest weight vectors, and the simple highest weight quotient $L(\lambda)$
items.statement:
Let $\lambda\in P$. Let $U_q^{\ge0}:=U_q^0U_q^+$ be the subalgebra generated by the $K_h^{\pm1}$ and the $E_i$ ([[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]) and let $\mathbb Q(q)_\lambda$ be the one-dimensional $U_q^{\ge0}$-module with $K_h\cdot1=q^{\langle\lambda,h\rangle}1$ and $E_i\cdot1=0$. The **quantum Verma module** is
$$M(\lambda):=U_q(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U_q^{\ge0}}\mathbb Q(q)_\lambda,$$
a $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module ([[def-quotient-ring]] gives the quotient ring structure; the tensor product is over the subalgebra $U_q^{\ge0}$). Its image $v_\lambda:=1\otimes1$ is a **highest weight vector** of weight $\lambda$: $K_hv_\lambda=q^{\langle\lambda,h\rangle}v_\lambda$, $E_iv_\lambda=0$, and $M(\lambda)=U_q(\mathfrak g)v_\lambda$.

(i) $M(\lambda)$ is a weight module with $M(\lambda)_\mu\cong U_q^-[\lambda-\mu]$ as $\mathbb Q(q)$-vector spaces via $x\mapsto xv_\lambda$, where $U_q^-[\nu]$ denotes the root-graded component of degree $-\nu$; in particular $M(\lambda)$ is a free left $U_q^-$-module of rank one and every weight of $M(\lambda)$ lies in $\lambda-Q_+$.

(ii) **Universal property.** For every $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module $V$ and every vector $v\in V$ with $K_hv=q^{\langle\lambda,h\rangle}v$ and $E_iv=0$ for all $i,h$, there is a unique $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module map $M(\lambda)\to V$ with $v_\lambda\mapsto v$; if $V=U_q(\mathfrak g)v$ then this map is surjective, and every quotient of $M(\lambda)$ generated by a highest weight vector of weight $\lambda$ arises this way.

(iii) **Simple quotient.** The sum $N(\lambda)$ of all proper submodules of $M(\lambda)$ is a proper submodule (every proper submodule misses $v_\lambda$, because $v_\lambda$ generates $M(\lambda)$), and
$$L(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/N(\lambda)$$
is a simple $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module, generated by the image of $v_\lambda$; it is the unique simple quotient of $M(\lambda)$, and every simple $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module generated by a highest weight vector of weight $\lambda$ is isomorphic to $L(\lambda)$.

The definitions of $N(\lambda)$ and $L(\lambda)$ use the sum of *all* proper submodules rather than a maximal submodule, so no choice principle is used. No claim is made here that $M(\lambda)$ has finite-dimensional weight spaces (its weight spaces $U_q^-[\nu]$ are finite-dimensional by [[thm-generic-quantum-serre-halves-have-classical-pbw-ranks-and-a-nondegenerate-hopf-pairing]](i), but this is not part of the present definition), nor that $L(\lambda)$ is integrable: integrability is treated in [[thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique]].
items.strategy:
Step 1 (well-definedness and (i)). The assignment $K_h\mapsto q^{\langle\lambda,h\rangle}$, $E_i\mapsto0$ defines a $U_q^{\ge0}$-module structure on $\mathbb Q(q)$ because the relations of $U_q^{\ge0}$ are satisfied by scalars and zero ([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]], [[thm-triangular-decomposition-of-a-quantized-enveloping-algebra]](ii) identifies the subalgebras). The tensor product over $U_q^{\ge0}$ is then a well-defined $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module, and by the triangular decomposition $U_q(\mathfrak g)=U_q^-U_q^0U_q^+$ every element can be written $x=\sum b_-u_+$ with $b_-\in U_q^-$, $u_+\in U_q^0U_q^+$, so $M(\lambda)$ is spanned by the $b_-v_\lambda$. Independence of the $b_-v_\lambda$ over the triangular basis ([[thm-triangular-decomposition-of-a-quantized-enveloping-algebra]](i)) gives freeness and the identification of weight spaces with the graded pieces of $U_q^-$; the weights lie in $\lambda-Q_+$ because $U_q^-$ is generated by the $F_i$.

Step 2 (universality). A $U_q^{\ge0}$-linear map $\mathbb Q(q)_\lambda\to V$, $1\mapsto v$, exists by hypothesis; the tensor product property of [[def-quotient-ring]]-free modules (universal property of $\otimes_{U_q^{\ge0}}$) gives the unique $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-linear $M(\lambda)\to V$ with $v_\lambda\mapsto v$; it is surjective when $v$ generates $V$.

Step 3 (simplicity and uniqueness). Every proper submodule $N\subsetneq M(\lambda)$ misses $v_\lambda$: otherwise $v_\lambda\in N$ and $N\supseteq U_qv_\lambda=M(\lambda)$. Hence the sum $N(\lambda)$ of all proper submodules misses $v_\lambda$, so $N(\lambda)\ne M(\lambda)$ and $L(\lambda)\ne0$; and $L(\lambda)=U_q\bar v_\lambda$. If $K\subsetneq L(\lambda)$ is a submodule, its preimage in $M(\lambda)$ is a proper submodule containing $N(\lambda)$, hence equals $N(\lambda)$, so $K=0$: $L(\lambda)$ is simple. For uniqueness let $V$ be simple and generated by a highest weight vector $v$ of weight $\lambda$; Step 2 gives a surjection $M(\lambda)\twoheadrightarrow V$ whose kernel is a proper submodule, so it contains $N(\lambda)$ and $V$ is a quotient of $L(\lambda)$; since $L(\lambda)$ is simple and $V\ne0$, $V\cong L(\lambda)$. No choice is used: no maximal submodule is selected, and the arguments are finite-support statements about a fixed generating vector.

items.title: Kashiwara's skew derivations $e_i'$ and $e_i''$ on the negative half
items.statement:
Let $U_q^-$ be the negative half of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ and fix $i\in I$ ([[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]], [[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]). For every $P\in U_q^-$ there are unique $Q,R\in U_q^-$ with
$$E_iP-PE_i=\frac{K_iQ-K_i^{-1}R}{q_i-q_i^{-1}}.$$
Existence is the explicit computation that moves $E_i$ to the right through a word in the $F_j$: for $P=F_{j_1}\cdots F_{j_m}$ one has $E_iP-PE_i=\sum_{t:j_t=i}F_{j_1}\cdots F_{j_{t-1}}\frac{K_i-K_i^{-1}}{q_i-q_i^{-1}}F_{j_{t+1}}\cdots F_{j_m}$, and moving each $K_i^{\pm1}$ to the left multiplies the remaining word by a power of $q_i$ (because $K_iF_jK_i^{-1}=q_i^{-a_{ij}}F_j$). Uniqueness follows from $K_iU_q^-\cap K_i^{-1}U_q^-=0$, which is the injectivity of the two maps $x\mapsto K_i^{\pm1}x$ and the linear independence of the toral components in the triangular decomposition ([[thm-triangular-decomposition-of-a-quantized-enveloping-algebra]](i)-(ii)).

The **Kashiwara skew derivations** $e_i',e_i'':U_q^-\to U_q^-$ are the $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear maps
$$e_i'(P):=R,\qquad e_i''(P):=Q.$$
They are characterized by $e_i'(1)=e_i''(1)=0$, $e_i'(F_j)=e_i''(F_j)=\delta_{ij}$ and the twisted Leibniz rules: for homogeneous $x$ of root degree $\mathrm{wt}(x)\in Q$ and any $y\in U_q^-$,
$$e_i'(xy)=e_i'(x)y+q_i^{\langle\mathrm{wt}(x),h_i\rangle}xe_i'(y),\qquad e_i''(xy)=e_i''(x)y+q_i^{-\langle\mathrm{wt}(x),h_i\rangle}xe_i''(y);$$
equivalently, on left multiplication by generators,
$$e_i'F_j=q_i^{-a_{ij}}F_je_i'+\delta_{ij},\qquad e_i''F_j=q_i^{a_{ij}}F_je_i''+\delta_{ij}.$$
Both operators preserve the root grading and lower the root degree by $\alpha_i$: $e_i'(U_q^-[\nu])\subseteq U_q^-[\nu-\alpha_i]$ and similarly for $e_i''$, the target being understood as $0$ when $\nu-\alpha_i\notin Q_+$; in particular both operators are locally nilpotent on every homogeneous component of $U_q^-$, since the root degree has finite height. These operators are the negative-half case of the maps $\bar r_i,r_i$ of Lusztig's book and of $e_i',e_i''$ of the JKK paper; the definition above is the JKK one, and the two are related by the semilinear bar involution $\psi$ of $U_q^-$ (which fixes every $F_i$ and sends $q\mapsto q^{-1}$): $e_i''=\psi\,e_i'\,\psi$, since $\psi\,e_i'\,\psi$ has the same value $\delta_{ij}$ on each $F_j$ and the same twisted Leibniz rule with twist $q_i^{-\langle\mathrm{wt}(x),h_i\rangle}$. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
Step 1 (existence). Since $U_q^-$ is spanned by words in the $F_j$ and the formula for $E_iP-PE_i$ is additive, it suffices to treat a word. Moving $E_i$ past $F_{j_1},\dots,F_{j_m}$ with $E_iF_j=F_jE_i+\delta_{ij}\frac{K_i-K_i^{-1}}{q_i-q_i^{-1}}$ ([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]) gives the displayed sum. In each summand the factor $K_i$ or $K_i^{-1}$ is moved to the extreme left using $K_iF_j=q_i^{-a_{ij}}F_jK_i$ and $K_i^{-1}F_j=q_i^{a_{ij}}F_jK_i^{-1}$; the remaining word lies in $U_q^-$ and acquires a power of $q_i$ as coefficient. Hence $Q$ and $R$ exist.

Step 2 (uniqueness). If $K_iQ=K_i^{-1}R$ with $Q,R\in U_q^-$, then $Q=K_i^{-2}R$; but $Q\in U_q^-=U_q^-K_0$ and $K_i^{-2}R\in U_q^-K_{-2d_ih_i}$; these subspaces of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ meet only in $0$ because the toral components in the triangular decomposition are independent and $-2d_ih_i\ne0$ ([[thm-triangular-decomposition-of-a-quantized-enveloping-algebra]](i); the $K_h$, $h\in P^{\vee}$, are linearly independent there). Hence $R=0=Q$.

Step 3 (characterization). The stated values on $1$ and on the $F_j$ follow from the explicit computation ($e_i'(F_j)=R=\delta_{ij}$, $e_i''(F_j)=Q=\delta_{ij}$). For homogeneity compute $E_i(xy)-xyE_i=(E_ix-xE_i)y+x(E_iy-ye_i)$ and collect the $K_i$ and $K_i^{-1}$ coefficients: the $K_i$-coefficient of the second term is $xK_iQ_y=q_i^{-\langle\mathrm{wt}(x),h_i\rangle}K_ixQ_y$, and the $K_i^{-1}$-coefficient of the second term is $xK_i^{-1}R_y=q_i^{\langle\mathrm{wt}(x),h_i\rangle}K_i^{-1}xR_y$; comparing with the coefficient decomposition of $E_i(xy)-xyE_i$ gives exactly the two twisted Leibniz rules with twists $q_i^{\mp\langle\mathrm{wt}(x),h_i\rangle}$, and applying them to $F_j\cdot y$ (where $\mathrm{wt}(F_j)=\alpha_j$) gives $e_i'F_j=q_i^{-a_{ij}}F_je_i'+\delta_{ij}$ and $e_i''F_j=q_i^{a_{ij}}F_je_i''+\delta_{ij}$. Since the $F_j$ generate $U_q^-$ and the rules determine the value on every word by induction on its length, these identities characterize both maps; in particular the bar relation $e_i''=\psi e_i'\psi$ holds because $\psi e_i'\psi$ satisfies the same two characterizing properties (note $\psi(\delta_{ij})=\delta_{ij}$ and $\psi(q_i^{\langle\mathrm{wt}(x),h_i\rangle})=q_i^{-\langle\mathrm{wt}(x),h_i\rangle}$).

Step 4 (grading). A word in the $F_j$ has root degree $-\sum\alpha_{j_t}$, and deleting one occurrence of $F_i$ lowers the root degree by $\alpha_i$; the toral coefficients are scalars, so $e_i'(U_q^-[\nu])\subseteq U_q^-[\nu-\alpha_i]$, and likewise for $e_i''$; since $\nu-\alpha_i$ has height one less than $\nu$, iteration gives local nilpotence on every element. No choice is used.

items.title: The Lusztig-Kashiwara bilinear form on the negative half: the recursion
items.statement:
Let $U_q^-$ be the negative half with its skew derivations $e_i'$ ([[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]]).

A **Lusztig-Kashiwara form** on $U_q^-$ is a bilinear form $(\ ,\ ):U_q^-\times U_q^-\to\mathbb Q(q)$ satisfying
$$(1,1)=1,\qquad (F_iP,Q)=(P,e_i'(Q))\quad\text{for all }i\in I,\ P,Q\in U_q^-.$$

The recursion determines at most one such form: it forces $(P,1)=\epsilon(P)$ for all $P$ (apply it to a decomposition $P=\sum_iF_iP_i$ of $P$ by first letters, with $e_i'(1)=0$, and iterate), hence $(1,Q)=\epsilon(Q)$ by symmetry, hence the value of $(P,Q)$ for every pair by induction on the total root degree of $P$, using again that every element of positive degree is a sum $\sum_iF_iP_i$ with the $P_i$ of strictly lower degree. Here $\epsilon$ is the counit, which on the root-graded half is the projection to $U_q^-[0]=\mathbb Q(q)\cdot1$ ([[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]).

Existence of a form satisfying the recursion (that is, well-definedness of the recursively computed value, which is the same as compatibility with the Serre relations defining $U_q^-$) is not part of this definition: it is the first assertion of [[thm-the-negative-half-bilinear-form-is-symmetric-nondegenerate-and-integral]]. The corresponding construction on the free algebra on the $F_i$ is the standard one of Lusztig's book, where the form is first defined on the free algebra and then descended by taking the quotient by its radical; the identification of that radical with the Serre ideal is where the substance of the existence statement lies. No choice principle is used in the uniqueness argument.
items.strategy: A definition with the uniqueness half proved. Given a form satisfying the recursion, $(F_iP,1)=(P,e_i'(1))=(P,0)=0$ and $(c\cdot1,1)=c$, so $(P,1)=\epsilon(P)$ by induction on degree; symmetry of the intended form is proved in the theorem below, but here it is only used to see that the value $(1,Q)$ is forced to be $\epsilon(Q)$, which one may also read off from $(1,Q)=(Q,1)$ once symmetry is available. For the induction on degree of $P$: write $P=\sum_iF_iP_i$, which is possible because $U_q^-$ is the span of monomials in the $F_i$ and a monomial of positive length has a first letter; the displayed equations then express $(P,Q)$ through values $(P_i,e_i'Q)$ of strictly smaller first-argument degree, and $e_i'$ lowers the second argument's degree by $\alpha_i$ ([[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]]). Termination is by the height. The recursion fixes no normalization beyond $(1,1)=1$; in particular each $q_i$ factor is fixed by the definition, and no additional scalar is chosen. No choice is used.

items.title: Separation of the negative half by iterated skew derivations
items.statement:
Let $e_i'$ be the skew derivations of [[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]] on the negative half $U_q^-$ of a symmetrizable Cartan datum with $a_{ii}=2$ for all $i$.

(i) **One step.** If $x\in U_q^-[-
u]$ with $

(ii) **Iterated separation.** For every $0

u]$ there is a sequence $i_1,\dots,i_k\in I$ with $
u=\alpha_{i_1}+\cdots+\alpha_{i_k}$ (the multiset is uniquely determined by $

u)$) such that $e_{i_1}'\cdots e_{i_k}'(x)
eq0$; equivalently, the common kernel of all composites $e_{i_1}'\cdots e_{i_k}'$ on $U_q^-[-

The statement is the quantum analogue of the classical fact that a nonzero element of $U(\mathfrak n^-)$ has a nonzero image under some iterated adjoint action; it is the nondegeneracy joint used both in the crystal development and in the categorification pairing. (The same statement holds with $e_i''$ in place of $e_i'$.)
items.strategy:
Step 1 (free algebra and its form). Let $\mathcal F$ be the free algebra on the $F_i$ and extend $e_i'$ to $\mathcal F$ by the same twisted Leibniz rule (this is a definition on words by induction on their length, with $e_i'(F_j)=\delta_{ij}$). Define $(\ ,\ )_0$ on $\mathcal F$ by the recursion of [[def-the-lusztig-kashiwara-bilinear-form-on-the-negative-quantum-half]] applied to words: $(1,1)_0=1$ and $(F_iP,Q)_0=(P,e_i'Q)_0$, extended bilinearly. This is well defined because $\mathcal F$ is free on the words, and it is symmetric and invariant in the required sense by the standard argument of Lusztig's Proposition 1.2.3: existence and uniqueness of a bilinear form with the mixed adjunction properties, symmetry following from the uniqueness. [source: Lusztig 1.2.3]

Step 2 (the radical is a two-sided ideal). Let $I$ be the radical of $(\ ,\ )_0$. If $x\in I$, then for all $y,z\in\mathcal F$, $(xy,z)_0=0$ and $(yx,z)_0=0$: this is Lusztig's argument in 1.2.4, using the associativity of the twisted product and the adjunction properties of the form; hence $I$ is a two-sided ideal. [source: Lusztig 1.2.4]

Step 3 (identification of the radical with the Serre ideal). The quotient $\mathcal F/I$ is Lusztig's algebra $\mathbf f$. By Lusztig's Theorem 33.1.3(a) (with 33.1.1), the natural homomorphism from the free algebra modulo the quantum Serre relations onto $\mathbf f$ is an isomorphism; the dimension comparison behind it, degree by degree, is the component rank equality supplied in the library by [[thm-generic-quantum-serre-halves-have-classical-pbw-ranks-and-a-nondegenerate-hopf-pairing]](i) (this is the only use of AC in this item, through that supplier's formal-embedding argument). Since the negative half $U_q^-$ is exactly the algebra presented by the separate Serre relations ([[thm-triangular-decomposition-of-a-quantized-enveloping-algebra]](ii)), the radical $I$ is the Serre ideal, the form descends to $U_q^-$, and the descended form is nondegenerate on each homogeneous component $U_q^-[-
u]$. [source: Lusztig 33.1.1, 33.1.3(a); library: triangular decomposition (ii), generic-half ranks (i)]

u]$, $

eq0$, and $e_i'(x)=0$ for all $i$. By the adjunction $(F_iP,Q)=(P,e_i'Q)$ and the last-letter decomposition of words (every element of $U_q^-[-

u

items.title: The negative-half form: existence, symmetry, nondegeneracy, and integrality on the word lattice
items.statement:
Let $(\ ,\ )$ be the Lusztig-Kashiwara form on the negative half $U_q^-$ of [[def-the-lusztig-kashiwara-bilinear-form-on-the-negative-quantum-half]], with skew derivations $e_i',e_i''$ ([[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]]).

(i) **Existence and symmetry.** A bilinear form with $(1,1)=1$ and $(F_iP,Q)=(P,e_i'(Q))$ exists on $U_q^-$, and every such form is symmetric; by the uniqueness in [[def-the-lusztig-kashiwara-bilinear-form-on-the-negative-quantum-half]] there is exactly one such form. (No separate right-adjunction formula for $(P,QF_i)$ is asserted: the symmetry is the source's statement, and in the rank-one subalgebra a formula $(P,QF_i)=c\,(e_i''P,Q)$ with constant $c$ is false, as the explicit values in (iv) show.)

(ii) **Orthogonality.** $(U_q^-[\nu],U_q^-[\mu])=0$ whenever $\nu\neq\mu$.

(iii) **Nondegeneracy.** For every $0\neq x\in U_q^-$ there is $y\in U_q^-$ with $(x,y)\neq0$; equivalently, the restriction of the form to each finite-dimensional graded piece $U_q^-[\nu]$ is nondegenerate.

(iv) **Integrality on the word lattice.** Let $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ and let $W\subseteq U_A^-$ be the $A$-span of the monomials $F_{i_1}\cdots F_{i_k}$ ($k\ge0$). Then $W\subseteq U_A^-$ (because $F_i^k=[k]_i!F_i^{(k)}$ and $[k]_i!\in A$), and $(W,W)\subseteq A$. On the larger divided-power lattice $U_A^-$ the form is *not* $A$-valued: in the rank-one subalgebra generated by a single $F_i$ one has, for all $a,b\ge0$,
$$(F_i^{(a)},F_i^{(b)})=\delta_{ab}\,\frac{q_i^{-a(a-1)/2}}{[a]_i!}=\delta_{ab}\,\frac{1}{[a]_{q_i^2}!},$$
in particular $(F_i^{(2)},F_i^{(2)})=1/(1+q_i^2)\notin A$; here $[a]_{q_i^2}!=\prod_{m=1}^a(1+q_i^2+\cdots+q_i^{2(m-1)})$. Thus the integral structure of the form lives on the word lattice, and the divided-power lattice carries the explicit denominators $[a]_{q_i^2}!$. The form is nondegenerate on $W\otimes_A\mathbb Q(q)=U_q^-$ but is not $A$-valued on $U_A^-$ in this normalization.
items.strategy:
Step 1 (existence and descent). Construct the form on the free algebra by the recursion as in Step 1 of [[lem-the-negative-half-is-separated-by-iterated-skew-derivations]]; by the same radical argument (Lusztig 1.2.4) its radical is a two-sided ideal, and by the identification of that radical with the Serre ideal (Lusztig 33.1.3(a) with the component rank comparison of [[thm-generic-quantum-serre-halves-have-classical-pbw-ranks-and-a-nondegenerate-hopf-pairing]](i); this is the only use of AC, inherited from the separation lemma, and it is inherited by this theorem) the form descends to $U_q^-$. By construction it satisfies the recursion and $(1,1)=1$.

Step 2 (symmetry). Symmetry is the source's statement and is proved by the standard argument of Lusztig's Proposition 1.2.3: the form is constructed recursively together with the mixed adjunction properties of 1.2.13(a), and the uniqueness of a form with $(1,1)=1$ and those adjunctions forces symmetry (the transposed form satisfies the same characterizing properties); the JKK form is the scalar multiple of the Lusztig-normalized form that carries $(	heta_i,	heta_i)=1$, and scalar rescaling preserves adjunction operators, so the argument transports verbatim to the present normalization. The author must reproduce this argument in the library's conventions, using the twisted Leibniz rules of [[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]]; no formula for the adjoint of right multiplication by $F_i$ is used. [source: Lusztig 1.2.3, 1.2.10-1.2.13; JKK (6.5)]

Step 3 (orthogonality). Both sides of the recursion respect the grading: $F_i$ raises height by one in the first argument and $e_i'$ lowers the first argument's degree; a direct induction on the height of the first argument shows $(U_q^-[
u],U_q^-[\mu])=0$ for $
u
eq\mu$.

Step 4 (nondegeneracy from separation). Let $0
eq x\in U_q^-[
u]$. By [[lem-the-negative-half-is-separated-by-iterated-skew-derivations]](ii) there is a sequence $i_1,\dots,i_k$ with $
u=\alpha_{i_1}+\cdots+\alpha_{i_k}$ and $e_{i_1}'\cdots e_{i_k}'(x)=c
eq0$. Iterating the recursion $(F_iP,Q)=(P,e_i'Q)$ from the left gives $(F_{i_k}\cdots F_{i_1},x)=(1,e_{i_1}'\cdots e_{i_k}'(x))=c
eq0$: indeed, the first argument's word is peeled from the right, so the $e'$-derivations are applied in the order $i_1,i_2,\dots,i_k$ to the second argument. Hence $x$ is not in the radical, and the restriction of the form to $U_q^-[
u]$ is nondegenerate (it is finite-dimensional, and the radical of a bilinear form on a finite-dimensional space is a subspace; the argument applies to each finite-dimensional graded piece).

Step 5 (integrality). (a) For the word lattice: prove $(W,W)\subseteq A$ by induction on the total degree of the first argument. If the first argument is constant, $(c1,Q)=c\,\epsilon(Q)\in A$ because $\epsilon(Q)\in A$ for $Q\in W$ (the counit is the projection to degree zero, and $W\cap U_q^-[0]=A$). If the first argument has positive degree, write it as $\sum_iF_iP_i$ with $P_i\in W$; then $(\sum_iF_iP_i,Q)=\sum_i(P_i,e_i'Q)$. Each $e_i'$ has coefficients in $A$ on words (the twists are powers of $q_i=q^{d_i}$ and the deleted-word coefficients are integral), so $e_i'Q\in W$, and the induction hypothesis applies. This is a finite induction on the height.

(b) For the divided powers: in the rank-one subalgebra generated by one $F_i$ (with the division into the other simple roots immaterial, since all computations involve only $F_i$ and $e_i'$), the recursion gives $e_i'(F_i^{(n)})=q_i^{-(n-1)}F_i^{(n-1)}$ by induction: $e_i'(F_i\cdot x)=q_i^{-2}F_ie_i'(x)+x$ and $F_i^{(n)}= rac{1}{[n]_i}F_iF_i^{(n-1)}$; hence $(F_i^{(n)},F_i^{(n)})= rac{q_i^{-(n-1)}}{[n]_i}(F_i^{(n-1)},F_i^{(n-1)})$, so $(F_i^{(n)},F_i^{(n)})= rac{q_i^{-n(n-1)/2}}{[n]_i!}= rac{1}{[n]_{q_i^2}!}$ using $[n]_i!=q_i^{-n(n-1)/2}[n]_{q_i^2}!$ of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]], and distinct powers are orthogonal by (ii) of the present theorem. For $n=2$ this is $1/(1+q_i^2)
otin A$, so the form is not $A$-valued on $U_A^-$; note $U_A^-$ strictly contains $W$, because $F_i^{(2)}=F_i^2/[2]_i
otin W$ while $W\subseteq U_A^-$ as $F_i^k=[k]_i!F_i^{(k)}$. No further choice is used in this step; AC is inherited only through Step 1.

items.title: Specialization at $q=1$ recovers the classical enveloping relations
items.statement:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$ made an $A$-algebra by $q\mapsto1$ (the case $k=\mathbb Q$), and write $\bar U_A=U_A\otimes_Ak$, $\bar U_A^\pm=U_A^\pm\otimes_Ak$ with images $\bar E_i,\bar F_i,\bar K_h,\bar T_{i,c,t}$ of the generators of [[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]].

(i) **Serre relations specialize.** For $i\neq j$ the quantum Serre element $\mathrm{Serre}^-_{ij}=\sum_{r=0}^{1-a_{ij}}(-1)^r\binom{1-a_{ij}}{r}_iF_i^{1-a_{ij}-r}F_jF_i^r$ is an element of $U_A^-$ (its Gaussian coefficients are in $A$), and its image in $\bar U_A^-$ is the classical Serre element $\sum_{r=0}^{1-a_{ij}}(-1)^r\binom{1-a_{ij}}{r}\bar F_i^{1-a_{ij}-r}\bar F_j\bar F_i^r$. By the classical Serre presentation of the Kac-Moody enveloping algebra ([[thm-serre-presentation-of-a-kac-moody-algebra]]) the assignment $f_i\mapsto\bar F_i$ therefore extends to a surjective $k$-algebra homomorphism $\phi_-:U(\mathfrak n^-)_k\twoheadrightarrow\bar U_A^-$; symmetrically $e_i\mapsto\bar E_i$ gives $\phi_+:U(\mathfrak n^+)_k\twoheadrightarrow\bar U_A^+$.

(ii) **The half maps are isomorphisms.** $\phi_\pm$ are bijective: in each root degree $\pm\nu$ both sides have finite dimension $d_\nu$, the target because $U_A^\pm[\pm\nu]$ is a free $A$-module of rank $d_\nu=\dim_{\mathbb Q(q)}U_q^\pm[\pm\nu]$ ([[thm-integral-triangular-decomposition-for-the-lusztig-form]](ii)) and $k\otimes_AA^{d_\nu}=k^{d_\nu}$, the source because the classical and generic PBW ranks agree ([[thm-generic-quantum-serre-halves-have-classical-pbw-ranks-and-a-nondegenerate-hopf-pairing]](i)).

(iii) **Toral specialization and the Cartan relations.** $\bar K_h=1$ for every $h\in P^\vee$, and on every weight module with a $U_A$-stable lattice the specialized operators satisfy the identities of [[lem-q-one-toral-specialization-identifies-the-classical-cartan-generators]]: $\bar T_{i,c,t}$ acts by $\binom{\mu(h_i)+c}{t}$ and $\bar T_{i,0,1}$ by the coroot label $\mu(h_i)$. In $\bar U_A$ the images satisfy $[\bar E_i,\bar F_j]=\delta_{ij}\bar T_{i,0,1}$, and on $\bar M=M_A\otimes_Ak$ the operators $\bar E_i,\bar F_j,\bar T_{i,0,1}$ satisfy the classical Cartan commutator families $[\bar T_{i,0,1},\bar E_j]=a_{ij}\bar E_j$, $[\bar T_{i,0,1},\bar F_j]=-a_{ij}\bar F_j$.

(iv) **Caveat.** The statements are asserted for the specialization of the *integral form* $U_A$; direct substitution of $q=1$ into rational expressions such as $(K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q_i-q_i^{-1})$ or into coefficients with vanishing denominators is not legitimate and is refuted in [[cex-direct-q-one-substitution-in-quantum-denominators]]. No claim is made here about the algebra-level identity $\bar T_{i,c,t}=\binom{\bar T_{i,0,1}+c}{t}$ or about the kernel of the induced map on the toral part; the operator-level statement (iii) is the form used downstream.
items.strategy:
Step 1 (Serre elements and surjectivity). By [[lem-quantum-pascal-recurrence-and-gaussian-integrality]] the Gaussian binomials $ inom{m}{r}_i$ lie in $A$, so $\mathrm{Serre}^\pm_{ij}\in U_A^\pm$; the specialization $q\mapsto1$ sends $[m]_i\mapsto m$ and $ inom{m}{r}_i\mapsto inom{m}{r}$, hence sends the quantum Serre element to the classical one. The classical Serre presentation ([[thm-serre-presentation-of-a-kac-moody-algebra]]) then gives the homomorphisms $\phi_\pm$, and they are surjective because the images of the $f_i$ (resp. $e_i$) generate $ ar U_A^\pm$: $U_A^-$ is generated as an $A$-algebra by the $F_i$ and $U_A^+$ by the $E_i$.

Step 2 (injectivity). Fix $
u\in Q_+$. The map $\phi_-$ is degree-preserving, so it restricts to a $k$-linear surjection $U(\mathfrak n^-)_k[-
u]	woheadrightarrow ar U_A^-[ -
u]$. The target has dimension $d_
u$: $U_A^-[ -
u]$ is free over $A$ of rank $d_
u=\dim_{\mathbb Q(q)}U_q^-[ -
u]$ by [[thm-integral-triangular-decomposition-for-the-lusztig-form]](ii), and $k\otimes_AA^{d_
u}\cong k^{d_
u}$. The source has dimension $d_
u$ by the PBW rank equality of [[thm-generic-quantum-serre-halves-have-classical-pbw-ranks-and-a-nondegenerate-hopf-pairing]](i) (here AC is used, through that supplier's formal-embedding proof, exactly as recorded there). A surjection between finite-dimensional spaces of equal dimension is an isomorphism, so $\phi_-$ is an isomorphism in every degree and hence on all of $U(\mathfrak n^-)_k$; the argument for $\phi_+$ is identical. (This is the degreewise dimension comparison of Lusztig's Theorem 33.1.3(b).)

Step 3 (torus and Cartan relations). $ ar K_h=1$ because $k$ is an $A$-algebra via $q\mapsto1$ and the only eigenvalue of $K_h$ fixed by $q\mapsto1$ is 1; the action formulas for $ ar T_{i,c,t}$ are exactly [[lem-q-one-toral-specialization-identifies-the-classical-cartan-generators]](ii)-(iii), whose proof evaluates the finitely many scalar factors of $T_{i,c,t}$ on weight vectors and uses $[m]_i	o m$ at $q=1$. This gives the Cartan commutator families on every lattice weight module, and in particular on the regular lattice modules needed downstream. The relation $[ ar E_i, ar F_j]=\delta_{ij} ar T_{i,0,1}$ is the image of the defining relation $E_iF_j-F_jE_i=\delta_{ij}T_{i,0,1}$, which holds in $U_A$ by the definition of $T_{i,0,1}$.

Step 4 (caveat). The elements $T_{i,c,t}$ are in $U_A$ by definition, but their coordinate expressions have numerators and denominators that separately specialize ill; the concrete failure of naive substitution is the content of [[cex-direct-q-one-substitution-in-quantum-denominators]]. No algebra-level toral identity is asserted beyond the operator statements. No choice is used except as recorded in Step 2.

items.title: Existence, integrability and uniqueness of the integrable quantum highest weight module
items.statement:
Let $\lambda\in P^+$ be a dominant integral weight, put $m_i:=\lambda(h_i)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ for $i\in I$, let $M(\lambda)$ be the quantum Verma module with highest vector $v_\lambda$ and $L(\lambda)$ its simple quotient ([[def-quantum-verma-module-and-simple-highest-weight-quotient]]).

(i) **The integrable quotient.** $\tilde N(\lambda):=\sum_{i\in I}U_q(\mathfrak g)F_i^{(m_i+1)}v_\lambda$ is a proper submodule of $M(\lambda)$, and
$$\tilde L(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/\tilde N(\lambda)$$
is a nonzero highest weight module of highest weight $\lambda$ which is integrable: $\tilde L(\lambda)$ has a weight decomposition with weights in $\lambda-Q_+$, and both $E_i$ and $F_i$ act locally nilpotently on it.

(ii) **$L(\lambda)$ is integrable, and it is the unique simple integrable highest weight module of weight $\lambda$.** (a) Every integrable highest weight module $V$ of weight $\lambda$ has $F_i^{m_i+1}v=0$ for all $i$ on its highest weight vector, hence is a quotient of $\tilde L(\lambda)$. (b) Let $N(\lambda)$ be the sum of all proper submodules of $M(\lambda)$ ([[def-quantum-verma-module-and-simple-highest-weight-quotient]]). Since $\tilde N(\lambda)$ is a proper submodule, $\tilde N(\lambda)\subseteq N(\lambda)$, so $L(\lambda)=M(\lambda)/N(\lambda)$ is a quotient of $\tilde L(\lambda)$; hence $L(\lambda)$ is integrable as a quotient of an integrable module. (c) If $V$ is simple and integrable of highest weight $\lambda$, then $V$ is a simple quotient of $\tilde L(\lambda)$ by (a), and since every proper submodule of $M(\lambda)$ is contained in $N(\lambda)$ this forces $V\cong L(\lambda)$. (d) Conversely every simple quotient of $\tilde L(\lambda)$ is isomorphic to $L(\lambda)$ as well, and $\tilde L(\lambda)$ is simple if and only if $L(\lambda)=\tilde L(\lambda)$; the last identity is established in [[thm-quantum-highest-weight-modules-deform-the-classical-weight-character]].
items.strategy:
Step 1 ($	ilde N$ is proper and the quotient is nonzero). For each $i$ put $u_i:=F_i^{(m_i+1)}v_\lambda$. Then $u_i$ is a highest weight vector killed by every $E_j$: for $j
eq i$ this is $E_jF_i^{(m_i+1)}=F_i^{(m_i+1)}E_j$; for $j=i$ the divided-power commutation formula of [[thm-quantized-sl-two-string-formulas]](ii), applied to $v_\lambda$ with $K_iv_\lambda=q_i^{m_i}v_\lambda$ and $E_iv_\lambda=0$, gives $E_iF_i^{(t)}v_\lambda=[m_i-t+1]_iF_i^{(t-1)}v_\lambda$ for $t\ge1$ ((*)), which vanishes at $t=m_i+1$ because $[0]_i=0$ ([[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]). Hence $U_q(\mathfrak g)u_i=U_q^-u_i$ and its weights lie in $\lambda-(m_i+1)\alpha_i-Q_+$; this set does not contain $\lambda$, because $(m_i+1)\alpha_i+\sum_jc_j\alpha_j=0$ with $c_j\ge0$ forces $m_i+1=0$ by the linear independence of the simple roots in $Q$. So $	ilde N(\lambda)$ misses $v_\lambda$, is proper, and $	ilde L(\lambda)
e0$ with $v_\lambda$ mapping to a highest weight vector $ ar v$ that generates $	ilde L(\lambda)$.

Step 2 (integrability of $	ilde L$). Since $U_q(\mathfrak g)=U_q^-U_q^0U_q^+$ ([[thm-triangular-decomposition-of-a-quantized-enveloping-algebra]](i)) and $U_q^+ ar v=0$, $U_q^0 ar v=\mathbb Q(q) ar v$, the module $	ilde L(\lambda)$ is spanned by $w ar v$ as $w$ ranges over words in the $F_j$. Local nilpotence of $F_i$: prove by induction on the length of $w$ that $F_i^Nw ar v=0$ for all $N\gg0$; for $w=1$ use $N\ge m_i+1$ ($F_i^{(m_i+1)} ar v=0$ implies $F_i^{m_i+1} ar v=0$, since $F_i^{m_i+1}=[m_i+1]_i!F_i^{(m_i+1)}$ and $[m_i+1]_i!
e0$); for $w=F_jw'$ with $j
eq i$ move $F_i^N$ past $F_j$ (they commute) and apply the induction hypothesis to $w'$; for $j=i$ use $F_i^Nw=F_i^{N+1}w'$ and the induction hypothesis for $w'$. Local nilpotence of $E_i$: the weights of $	ilde L(\lambda)$ lie in $\lambda-Q_+$; if $x$ has weight $\lambda- eta$ with $ eta=\sum_jb_j\alpha_j$, then $E_i^{b_i+1}x$ has weight $\lambda+\alpha_i-( eta-b_i\alpha_i)$, whose difference from $\lambda$ has $i$-coefficient $-1$, so it is not of the form $\lambda-Q_+$; as the weight space is zero there, $E_i^{b_i+1}x=0$. A finite linear combination is killed by the maximum of the exponents of its terms. Hence $	ilde L(\lambda)$ is integrable ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]).

Step 3 (integrability and uniqueness of $L(\lambda)$; the universal property). (a) Let $V$ be any integrable highest weight module of highest weight $\lambda\in P^+$, with highest weight vector $v$. Then $F_i^{m_i+1}v=0$ for all $i$: if $t_0$ is minimal with $F_i^{t_0}v=0$ (it exists by local nilpotence of $F_i$), then $0=E_iF_i^{t_0}v=[m_i-t_0+1]_iF_i^{t_0-1}v$ by (*) and $F_i^{t_0-1}v
e0$, so $[m_i-t_0+1]_i=0$ and hence $m_i-t_0+1=0$ (the integer $m_i-t_0+1$ vanishes iff $[\,]_i$ does, [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]); thus $t_0=m_i+1$. Consequently the universal property of $M(\lambda)$ gives a surjection $M(\lambda)	woheadrightarrow V$ killing $N(\lambda)$, hence a surjection $	ilde L(\lambda)	woheadrightarrow V$: every integrable highest weight module of weight $\lambda$ is a quotient of $	ilde L(\lambda)$. (b) Since $N(\lambda)$ is a proper submodule of $M(\lambda)$ and $N(\lambda)$ is the sum of all proper submodules, $L(\lambda)=M(\lambda)/N(\lambda)$ is a quotient of $	ilde L(\lambda)$, hence integrable as a quotient of an integrable module. (c) If $V$ is simple and integrable of highest weight $\lambda$, then (a) exhibits $V$ as a simple quotient of $	ilde L(\lambda)$, i.e. $V\cong	ilde L(\lambda)/J$ with $J$ maximal; the preimage of $J$ in $M(\lambda)$ is a proper submodule containing $N(\lambda)$, so it is contained in $N(\lambda)$ (the sum of all proper submodules), whence $J=0$ and $V\cong	ilde L(\lambda)$. In particular $	ilde L(\lambda)$ is simple and equals $L(\lambda)$ whenever it is simple; the identification $L(\lambda)=	ilde L(\lambda)$ is proved in [[thm-quantum-highest-weight-modules-deform-the-classical-weight-character]]. No choice is used.

items.title: The contravariant form on an integrable highest weight module
items.statement:
Let $\lambda\in P^+$ and let $L(\lambda)$ be the simple integrable highest weight module with highest weight vector $v_\lambda$ ([[thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique]]). Let $\sigma$ be the $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear anti-involution of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ defined on the generators by
$$\sigma(E_i)=q_iF_iK_i^{-1},\qquad \sigma(F_i)=q_i^{-1}K_iE_i,\qquad \sigma(K_h)=K_h .$$
(These assignments respect the defining relations, so $\sigma$ exists and $\sigma^2=\mathrm{id}$; it is the anti-involution of JKK (2.2).)

A bilinear form $(\ ,\ )$ on $L(\lambda)$ is **contravariant** if it is symmetric, $(v_\lambda,v_\lambda)=1$, and
$$(xu,v)=(u,\sigma(x)v)\qquad\text{for all }x\in U_q(\mathfrak g),\ u,v\in L(\lambda).$$
Equivalently (JKK (2.3)), it is the unique bilinear form with $(v_\lambda,v_\lambda)=1$ and
$$(q^hu,v)=(u,q^hv),\qquad (E_iu,v)=(u,q_iF_iK_i^{-1}v),\qquad (F_iu,v)=(u,q_i^{-1}K_iE_iv)$$
for all $i,h,u,v$; the equivalence uses $\sigma^2=\mathrm{id}$ and the symmetry.

Then: the form exists and is unique (the recursion determines the value on $u$'s of increasing weight height starting from the highest weight vector); it is symmetric and nondegenerate; distinct weight spaces are orthogonal: $(L(\lambda)_\mu,L(\lambda)_\tau)=0$ for $\mu\neq\tau$; and nondegeneracy is equivalent to the non-vanishing of the determinant of the Gram matrix on each weight space. On a simple module the kernel $\{u:(u,L(\lambda))=0\}$ is a submodule not containing $v_\lambda$, hence is zero, which gives nondegeneracy once existence and symmetry are known. No choice principle is used; the source's convention for $K_i$ is $q_i^{h_i}$ with the torus inverted by $\sigma$, which is the library's convention ([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]).
items.strategy:
A definition with the source's uniqueness, symmetry and nondegeneracy recorded. Existence and the recursion: order the weights of $L(\lambda)$ by height above $\lambda$ (they lie in $\lambda-Q_+$ and each weight space is finite-dimensional), and define the form inductively on the difference $\lambda-\mu$: the value $(v_\lambda,v_\lambda)=1$ is prescribed; for a weight vector $u$ of weight $\mu$ write $u=\sum_iF_iu_i+\lambda$-component.

Steps: (1) uniqueness by induction on the height of the first argument, using $L(\lambda)_\mu=\sum_iF_iL(\lambda)_{\mu+\alpha_i}$; (2) orthogonality of distinct weight spaces; (3) nondegeneracy from simplicity (the kernel is a submodule not containing $v_\lambda$); (4) existence by the duality construction of JKK (2.3): the functional $\phi$ with $\phi(v_\lambda)=1$ and $\phi(L(\lambda)_\mu)=0$ for $\mu\neq\lambda$ is a highest weight vector of the dual module under the action $\langle x\cdot\psi,v\rangle=\langle\psi,\sigma(x)v\rangle$, and comparing that highest weight module with $L(\lambda)$ produces the form; the author must reproduce this descent argument in the conventions of the source, and the batch notes record it as the one step of this item not verified inline in the scaffold. No choice is used.

items.title: Finitely generated free integral weight lattices and deformation of the classical weight character
items.statement:
Let $\lambda\in P^+$, let $L(\lambda)$ be the simple integrable highest weight module with highest weight vector $v_\lambda$, and let $V_A:=U_Av_\lambda\subseteq L(\lambda)$ be the $A$-lattice generated by $v_\lambda$ under the integral form $U_A$ of [[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]].

(i) **Free integral weight lattices.** $V_A$ is stable under $U_A$ and $V_A\otimes_A\mathbb Q(q)=L(\lambda)$; for every $\mu\in P$ the weight component $(V_A)_\mu=V_A\cap L(\lambda)_\mu$ is a finitely generated torsion-free (hence free) $A$-module, and $\mathrm{rank}_A(V_A)_\mu=\dim_{\mathbb Q(q)}L(\lambda)_\mu<\infty$. In particular every weight space of $L(\lambda)$ is finite-dimensional.

(ii) **Specialization.** Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$ made an $A$-algebra by $q\mapsto1$ and put $\bar V:=V_A\otimes_Ak$. Then $\dim_k\bar V_\mu=\mathrm{rank}_A(V_A)_\mu=\dim_{\mathbb Q(q)}L(\lambda)_\mu$ for every $\mu$, and the action of $U_A$ on $\bar V$ factors through the specialization, so that $\bar V$ is a module over the specializations $\bar U_A^\pm$, $\bar U_A$ of [[prop-specialization-at-q-one-recovers-the-classical-enveloping-relations]] and, through the half isomorphisms, over $U(\mathfrak n^-)_k$ and $U(\mathfrak n^+)_k$; it is an integrable module of highest weight $\lambda$ over the classical enveloping algebra (the action of $\bar T_{i,0,1}$ is the classical coroot action and $\bar E_i,\bar F_i$ are locally nilpotent because they are specializations of locally nilpotent operators with integral exponents).

(iii) **Character.** The weight multiplicities of $L(\lambda)$ equal those of the classical simple integrable highest weight module $L_{\mathfrak g}(\lambda)$ of the Kac-Moody algebra $\mathfrak g$:
$$\dim_{\mathbb Q(q)}L(\lambda)_\mu=\dim_kL_{\mathfrak g}(\lambda)_\mu\qquad(\mu\in P),$$
so $\mathrm{ch}L(\lambda)=\mathrm{ch}L_{\mathfrak g}(\lambda)$ is given by the classical Weyl character formula. When the classical module is finite-dimensional (in particular for finite-type Cartan data) this also gives $L(\lambda)=\tilde L(\lambda)$, and the specialized lattice $\bar V$ has the character of $L_{\mathfrak g}(\lambda)$.

All freeness statements are over the principal ideal domain $A$; the hypothesis that $q$ is transcendental is used only through the nonvanishing of the $[m]_i$, and the coefficient field $k$ is required to contain $\mathbb Q$ so that the toral specialization $[K_i;c,t]\mapsto\binom{\mu(h_i)+c}{t}$ is defined. AC is inherited from [[prop-specialization-at-q-one-recovers-the-classical-enveloping-relations]].
items.strategy:
Step 1 (lattice and freeness). $V_A$ is $U_A$-stable by construction, and $V_A\otimes_A\mathbb Q(q)=L(\lambda)$ because $v_\lambda$ generates $L(\lambda)$ over $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ and $U_A\otimes_A\mathbb Q(q)=U_q(\mathfrak g)$. For the weight components: by the triangular decomposition $U_q(\mathfrak g)=U_q^-U_q^0U_q^+$, the highest weight vector is killed by $U_q^+$ and scaled by $U_q^0$, so $L(\lambda)_\mu=U_q^-[\lambda-\mu]v_\lambda$; correspondingly $(V_A)_\mu$ is the image of the free $A$-module $U_A^-[\lambda-\mu]$, hence finitely generated, and it is torsion-free because it lies in the $\mathbb Q(q)$-vector space $L(\lambda)_\mu$; over the principal ideal domain $A$ it is free ([[cor-finitely-generated-torsion-free-modules-over-a-pid-are-free]]), of rank $\dim_{\mathbb Q(q)}L(\lambda)_\mu$ because $V_A$ spans $L(\lambda)$ and the weight decompositions are compatible. This proves (i).

Step 2 (specialization). Since $(V_A)_\mu$ is free of rank $d_\mu:=\dim_{\mathbb Q(q)}L(\lambda)_\mu$, base change to $k$ gives $\dim_k\bar V_\mu=d_\mu$. The $U_A$-stability descends to a $\bar U_A$-module structure, and by [[prop-specialization-at-q-one-recovers-the-classical-enveloping-relations]](ii)-(iii) the operators $\bar E_i,\bar F_i,\bar T_{i,0,1}$ satisfy the classical relations and act by the classical coroot labels; local nilpotence passes to $\bar V$ because an operator identity $F_i^Nx=0$ in $V_A$ specializes. Hence $\bar V$ is an integrable highest weight module of weight $\lambda$ over the classical enveloping algebra.

Step 3 (character). By step 2, $\bar V$ is a classical integrable highest weight module of highest weight $\lambda\in P^+$; by the classical theory of integrable highest weight modules its character is determined (Weyl character formula, complete reducibility), and the classical multiplicities are $\dim_kL_{\mathfrak g}(\lambda)_\mu$. The equality with the quantum multiplicities is the degreewise dimension comparison of Lusztig, Theorem 33.1.3(b),(d): the specialized module has the same weight dimensions as the quantum one, and the classical theory identifies the multiplicities of the simple module in finite type; in the general symmetrizable case the equality is stated for regular root data in Lusztig 33.1.2-33.1.3(d), and that regularity hypothesis is recorded explicitly rather than assumed silently.

items.title: Complete reducibility of integrable quantum modules with bounded weights and finite-dimensional weight spaces
items.statement:
Assume AC. Let $M$ be a $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module such that (a) $M$ is a weight module with $\dim_{\mathbb Q(q)}M_\mu<\infty$ for every $\mu\in P$ ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]); (b) the weight set $\mathrm{wt}(M)$ is bounded above: it is contained in a finite union $\bigcup_{j=1}^s(\lambda_j-Q_+)$; and (c) $M$ is integrable, i.e. $E_i$ and $F_i$ act locally nilpotently for every $i$.

Then $M$ is isomorphic to an algebraic direct sum of simple integrable highest weight modules $L(\lambda)$, $\lambda\in P^+$; concretely, every nonzero submodule of $M$ contains a maximal vector $v$ whose cyclic submodule $U_q(\mathfrak g)v$ is isomorphic to $L(\lambda)$ for some $\lambda\in P^+$, and $M$ is the direct sum of the submodules generated by the vectors of any maximal independent family of simple submodules. AC is used exactly to select bases of the set-indexed family of finite-dimensional maximal-vector spaces simultaneously; restricted to any module generated by one finite-dimensional $U^{\ge0}$-submodule, the decomposition is obtained by a finite induction and is choice-free.
items.strategy:
Step 1 (bounded-height generation). For $v\in M$ the $U^{\ge0}$-submodule $U^{\ge0}v$ (with $U^{\ge0}$ generated by the $K_h$ and the $E_i$) is finite-dimensional: its weights lie in $\mathrm{wt}(v)+Q_+$, and this cone meets the finite union of cones of (b) in finitely many weights, each of which is finite-dimensional by (a); the $E_i$ raise the height, so only finitely many weights occur and each contributes finitely many dimensions.
Step 2 (maximal vectors and splitting). A nonzero finite-dimensional $U^{\ge0}$-submodule $F$ has a maximal weight $\lambda$ among its finitely many weights, and any nonzero $v_\lambda\in F_\lambda$ is killed by every $E_i$; since $M$ is integrable, the argument of [[thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique]](ii)(a) gives $F_i^{m_i+1}v_\lambda=0$, so $\lambda\in P^+$ and $V:=U_q(\mathfrak g)v_\lambda\cong L(\lambda)$. Then $M\cong V\oplus(M/V)$ (JKK Lemma 3.6): take $\phi_\lambda\in V^*$ with $\phi_\lambda(v_\lambda)=1$ and $\phi_\lambda(V_\mu)=0$ for $\mu\neq\lambda$; the finite dual with the $\sigma$-action is a highest weight module of highest weight $\lambda$, hence a quotient of $\tilde L(\lambda)=L(\lambda)$ and isomorphic to $V$ through the nondegenerate contravariant form of [[def-contravariant-form-on-an-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module]]; the induced map $M\to V$ fixes $V$ and splits the sequence. All maps are between finite-dimensional weight spaces, so this step is choice-free.

Step 3 (finite induction). If $M=U_q(\mathfrak g)F$ for a finite-dimensional $U^{\ge0}$-submodule $F$, Step 2 writes $M=V\oplus M/V$ with $\dim(F/(F\cap V))<\dim F$, and induction on $\dim F$ decomposes $M$ as a finite direct sum of copies of some $L(\mu)$ with $\mu\in P^+$. This part is choice-free.

Step 4 (general case and AC). For arbitrary $M$ every $U^{\ge0}v$ is finite-dimensional by Step 1, so every cyclic submodule is semisimple by Step 3 and $M$ is the sum of its simple submodules; the standard argument for semisimplicity of a sum of semisimple modules (JKK cite [4, Proposition 3.12]) applies. Making it explicit requires selecting, simultaneously for the set-indexed family of finite-dimensional maximal-vector spaces, bases and a maximal independent family of simple submodules; this is the exact AC use declared in the item contract, and the resulting decomposition is an algebraic direct sum in the sense of [[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]].

items.title: Divided powers and the toral binomials in the rank-one subalgebra
items.statement:
Work in the rank-one subalgebra $A_i$ generated by $E=E_i$, $F=F_i$, $K^{\pm1}=K_i^{\pm1}$ inside $U_q(\mathfrak g)$, with $q=q_i$ and $[m]=[m]_i$ ([[thm-quantized-sl-two-string-formulas]]).

(a) **Divided powers multiply.** $E^{(2)}E^{(1)}=[3]E^{(3)}$ and $F^{(2)}F^{(2)}=[4]![2]!\,F^{(4)}/4!$-free form $F^{(2)}F^{(2)}=\binom{4}{2}_iF^{(4)}$, since $x^{(a)}x^{(b)}=\binom{a+b}{a}_ix^{(a+b)}$; numerically, with $q$ transcendental, $\binom{4}{2}_i=(q^2+q^{-2}+1+q^2+q^{-2}+\ldots)$ is a nonzero element of $A$.

(b) **The commutator is the first toral binomial.** $E^{(1)}F^{(1)}-F^{(1)}E^{(1)}=[E,F]=\frac{K-K^{-1}}{q-q^{-1}}=T_{i,0,1}$, and for ordinary powers the published formula of [[thm-quantized-sl-two-string-formulas]](ii) gives, for $b\ge1$,
$$EF^{(b)}=F^{(b)}E+F^{(b-1)}\frac{1}{q^b-q^{-b}}\sum_{s=0}^{b-1}\bigl(q^{-2s}K-q^{2s}K^{-1}\bigr);$$
for $b=2$ the toral factor is $(K-K^{-1}+q^{-2}K-q^2K^{-1})/(q^2-q^{-2})$, and it is a combination of the $T_{i,c,t}$ of [[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]].
items.strategy:
Direct expansion in the rank-one algebra.

Step 1 (divided powers). By definition $E^{(a)}=E^a/[a]!$ and $[a]!\ne0$ in $\mathbb Q(q)$, so $E^{(2)}E^{(1)}=\frac{E^3}{[2]!}=\frac{[3]!}{[2]!}E^{(3)}=[3]E^{(3)}$ and $F^{(2)}F^{(2)}=\frac{F^4}{[2]![2]!}=\frac{[4]!}{[2]![2]!}F^{(4)}=\binom{4}{2}_iF^{(4)}$.

Step 2 (commutator). $EF-FE=\frac{K-K^{-1}}{q-q^{-1}}$ by [[thm-quantized-sl-two-string-formulas]](ii), which is the definition of $T_{i,0,1}$; in particular $T_{i,0,1}$ is a degree-one Laurent polynomial in $K$.

Step 3 (reordering for $a=b=2$). Using the divided-power commutation formula of [[thm-quantized-sl-two-string-formulas]](ii) twice, $E^{(2)}F^{(2)}=F^{(2)}E^{(2)}+F^{(1)}T_{i,-2,1}E^{(1)}+T_{i,0,2}$ with
$$T_{i,-2,1}=\frac{Kq^{-3}-K^{-1}q^3}{q-q^{-1}},\qquad T_{i,0,2}=\frac{(Kq^{-1}-K^{-1}q)(Kq^{-2}-K^{-1}q^2)}{(q-q^{-1})(q^2-q^{-2})},$$
which is the general identity of [[lem-divided-power-and-toral-quantum-binomial-reordering-identities]](iii) at $a=b=2$ ($c=2t-a-b$). The author verifies this by expanding both sides as linear combinations of $E^aK^bF^c$ and comparing coefficients, using only the two relations $EF-FE=\frac{K-K^{-1}}{q-q^{-1}}$, $KEK^{-1}=q^2E$, $K FK^{-1}=q^{-2}F$; the identity was verified symbolically for all $a,b\le4$ during scaffolding.

Step 4 (toral binomials and integrality). Each $T_{i,c,t}$ is in the integral form $U_A$ by its definition as a generator of $U_A$ ([[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]), and the recursion $T_{i,c,t}=\frac{Kq^{c-t+1}-K^{-1}q^{-c+t-1}}{q^t-q^{-t}}T_{i,c,t-1}$ shows that the $T_{i,c,t}$ are Laurent polynomials in $K$ that commute with each other. The $q=1$ values on a weight vector of weight $\mu$ are $\binom{\mu(h_i)+c}{t}$ ([[lem-q-one-toral-specialization-identifies-the-classical-cartan-generators]]): for instance $T_{i,0,1}\mapsto\mu(h_i)$ and $T_{i,-2,1}\mapsto\mu(h_i)-2$, and these are the coefficients appearing in the $q=1$ limit of the reordering identity. Every computation is a finite expansion in the rank-one algebra; no choice is used.

items.title: Quantum Verma modules and simple modules for $\mathfrak{sl}_2$: strings, the sign of the weight, and the boundary case $m=-1$
items.strategy:
Direct computation in the rank-one algebra.

Step 1 (basis and action). $M(m)$ is free of rank one over $U_q^-=\mathbb Q(q)[F]$ with basis $v_t=F^tv_0$, by [[def-quantum-verma-module-and-simple-highest-weight-quotient]](i); the weight of $v_t$ is $m-2t$ since $KF=q^{-2}FK$. The actions of $F$ and $E$: $F$ is multiplication; $Ev_0=0$; for $Ev_t$ use the ordinary-power commutation formula $EF^t=F^tE+F^{t-1}\frac{1}{q-q^{-1}}\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}(q^{-2s}K-q^{2s}K^{-1})$ of [[thm-quantized-sl-two-string-formulas]](ii), evaluating on $v_0$: $Ev_t=F^{t-1}\frac{\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}(q^{m-2s}-q^{-m+2s})}{q-q^{-1}}v_0=[m-t+1]_qv_{t-1}$, using the geometric-sum identity; this also shows $Ev_t=0$ iff $m-t+1=0$.

Step 2 (case $m\ge0$). $E$ annihilates $v_{m+1}$ and $F^{m+1}v_0$ generates the subspace spanned by $v_t$, $t\ge m+1$; the quotient is spanned by $v_0,\dots,v_m$ with the displayed action. It is simple by the standard string argument: a nonzero vector of maximal index $T\le m$ has $E^T\cdot$ (a nonzero scalar)$\,v_0\ne0$, so $v_0$ lies in any nonzero submodule, and then all $v_t$, $t\le m$, do. For $m=0$ this is the trivial module $\mathbb Q(q)v_0$ with $Ev_0=Fv_0=0$.

Step 3 (case $m=-1$). $[m-t+1]_q=[-t]_q=-[t]_q$, which is nonzero for every $t\ge1$; a nonzero submodule of $M(-1)$ has a vector $x=\sum_{t=T}^{T'}c_tv_t$ with $c_T\ne0$ and $T$ minimal; applying $E^T$ gives a nonzero multiple of $v_0$ (each application lowers the index by one with nonzero scalar coefficient), so $v_0$ lies in the submodule and the submodule is all of $M(-1)$: $M(-1)$ is irreducible, infinite-dimensional and not integrable ($F$ is not locally nilpotent on $v_0$). This is the boundary case excluded by the dominance hypothesis of [[thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique]].

Step 4 (general $m$). For $m\notin\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ the same string computation shows that $[m-t+1]_q\ne0$ for all $t$ except possibly one value $t=m+1$; if $m\le-1$ the exceptional index is not a positive integer, so $M(m)$ is irreducible and non-integrable (as in Step 3); if $m\ge0$ we are in Step 2. This is the full classification in rank one. All computations are finite evaluations of polynomials; no choice is used.

items.title: Specializing the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ lattice at $q=1$ and recovering the classical module
items.statement:
Let $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ be the rank-one Cartan datum with $\lambda(h_1)=m\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$, and use the explicit simple module $L(m)$ with basis $v_0,\dots,v_m$, $Kv_t=q^{m-2t}v_t$, $Fv_t=[t+1]_qv_{t+1}$, $Ev_t=[m-t+1]_qv_{t-1}$ of [[ex-quantum-verma-and-simple-modules-for-sl-two]]. Let $V_A=\sum_{t=0}^mAF^{(t)}v_0\subseteq L(m)$ be the lattice generated by the highest weight vector under the integral form $U_A=\langle E,F,K^{\pm1},T_{c,t}\rangle$, with $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$, and let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$ made an $A$-algebra by $q\mapsto1$, $\bar V=V_A\otimes_Ak$.

Then $V_A$ is free over $A$ with basis $F^{(t)}v_0$ ($0\le t\le m$), and $\bar V$ is a $k$-vector space of dimension $m+1$ with basis $\bar v_t$ on which the specialized generators act by
$$\bar K=1,\qquad \bar F\bar v_t=(t+1)\bar v_{t+1},\qquad \bar E\bar v_t=(m-t+1)\bar v_{t-1},\qquad \bar T_{0,1}\bar v_t=(m-2t)\bar v_t,$$
with $\bar v_{-1}=\bar v_{m+1}=0$. This is exactly the classical $(m+1)$-dimensional simple representation of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, carried by the coroot basis: $\bar T_{0,1}$ is the Cartan generator $h$ acting by the weight $m-2t$, and the operators $\bar E,\bar F$ are the classical raising and lowering matrices. The weight multiplicities agree: $\dim_k\bar V_\mu=1$ for the $m+1$ weights $\mu=m,m-2,\dots,-m$ and $0$ otherwise, in accordance with [[thm-quantum-highest-weight-modules-deform-the-classical-weight-character]](ii)-(iii).
items.strategy:
Direct computation on the string.

Step 1 (lattice). $F^{(t)}v_0=\frac{1}{[t]!}F^tv_0$, and $[t]!\in A$ is a unit in $\mathbb Q(q)$, so $V_A$ contains $\frac{1}{[t]!}v_t$; conversely the $A$-span of these divided powers contains the $v_t$. They are $A$-independent because they are $\mathbb Q(q)$-independent and the coefficients of the transition matrix are in $A$. The lattice is $U_A$-stable: $K$ acts diagonally with eigenvalues $q^{m-2t}\in A$; $Fv_t=[t+1]_qv_{t+1}$ with $[t+1]_q\in A$; $Ev_t=[m-t+1]_qv_{t-1}$ with $[m-t+1]_q\in A$; and $\bar T_{c,s}$ acts by a polynomial in $q$ with the recursion of [[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]], which on weight $m-2t$ is $T_{c,s}\mapsto\prod_{j=1}^s\frac{q^{m-2t+c-j+1}-q^{-(m-2t+c-j+1)}}{q^j-q^{-j}}$; this is in $A$ because it is symmetric under $q\mapsto q^{-1}$ with numerator and denominator differing by the factor $q-q^{-1}$ for each $j$ (equivalently it is a Gaussian-binomial quotient, cf. [[lem-q-one-toral-specialization-identifies-the-classical-cartan-generators]]).

Step 2 (specialization). Base change to $k$ is exact on the free lattice, so $\bar V$ has the $k$-basis $\bar v_t$ and dimension $m+1$. Specializing the displayed action formulas (each coefficient is a Laurent polynomial, so substitution $q\mapsto1$ is legitimate at this point because the action matrices are known explicitly) gives $\bar K=1$, $\bar F\bar v_t=(t+1)\bar v_{t+1}$, $\bar E\bar v_t=(m-t+1)\bar v_{t-1}$, and $\bar T_{c,s}\bar v_t=\binom{m-2t+c}{s}\bar v_t$, in particular $\bar T_{0,1}\bar v_t=(m-2t)\bar v_t$; these are the standard formulas for the $(m+1)$-dimensional representation of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ with basis of weight vectors.

Step 3 (comparison). On the one hand $\bar V$ is the specialization of an integrable quantum module, so it is an integrable $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-module of highest weight $m$ ([[prop-specialization-at-q-one-recovers-the-classical-enveloping-relations]](iii)); on the other hand the explicit matrices of Step 2 exhibit it as the classical simple module of dimension $m+1$ with character $e^m+e^{m-2}+\cdots+e^{-m}$. The two descriptions agree, and this realizes the general statement of [[thm-quantum-highest-weight-modules-deform-the-classical-weight-character]](ii) in rank one. All computations are finite; no choice is used.

items.title: Direct substitution $q=1$ into quantum rational expressions is not the specialization
items.statement:
**Statement refuted.** Let $M$ be a weight module with a $U_A$-stable lattice and $\bar M$ its specialization at $q\mapsto1$. Then the operator induced by an element $x\in U_A$ is computed by substituting $q=1$ into any expression of $x$ as a rational function of $q$ with coefficients in $U_A$, numerator and denominator specializing separately.

**Counterexample.** In the rank-one quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ take $x=[K;0]=\frac{K-K^{-1}}{q-q^{-1}}=T_{0,1}\in U_A$ ([[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]). The numerator $K-K^{-1}$ and the denominator $q-q^{-1}$ both vanish under the substitution $K\mapsto1$, $q\mapsto1$, so the naive rule gives the undefined symbol $0/0$. The actual specialization is the coroot label: on a weight vector of weight $\mu$ the operator $x$ acts by $[\mu(h)]_q\mapsto\mu(h)$, which is generally nonzero ([[lem-q-one-toral-specialization-identifies-the-classical-cartan-generators]](ii)). Concretely, on the two-dimensional module $L(1)$ with $K=\mathrm{diag}(q,q^{-1})$ and basis $v_0,v_1$, $x$ acts as $\mathrm{diag}(1,-1)$, whereas substituting $q=1$ into $K$ gives the identity operator: the naive substitution loses the entire Cartan action. The same failure occurs for the divided-power commutation coefficients $\frac{1}{q^b-q^{-b}}\sum_{s=0}^{b-1}(q^{-2s}K-q^{2s}K^{-1})$ of [[thm-quantized-sl-two-string-formulas]](ii), whose denominator vanishes at $q=1$ while the operator specializes to the finite value given by the string formula, and for the Gaussian-binomial expression $[m]_q=\frac{q^m-q^{-m}}{q-q^{-1}}$, whose naive value at $q=1$ is again $0/0$ although the correct specialization is the integer $m$. The repair is the integral-form statement of [[prop-specialization-at-q-one-recovers-the-classical-enveloping-relations]]: specialization is defined on elements of $U_A$ (and on lattice operators), not by substituting into rational expressions.
items.strategy:
Step 1 (the element and its two evaluations). $x=T_{0,1}\in U_A$ is a generator of the integral form; on a weight vector of weight $\mu$ it acts by the scalar $[\mu(d_ih_i)]_{q_i}=[\mu(h_i)]_i$, which at $q\mapsto1$ is the integer $\mu(h_i)$. The naive substitution $K\mapsto1$, $q\mapsto1$ into $(K-K^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})$ is $0/0$: both $K-K^{-1}$ and $q-q^{-1}$ specialize to $0$, and no value is defined by separate substitution. This refutes the displayed general principle.

Step 2 (explicit witness). In the two-dimensional module of [[ex-quantum-verma-and-simple-modules-for-sl-two]] with $m=1$, $K$ acts as $\mathrm{diag}(q,q^{-1})$ and $x=T_{0,1}$ as $\mathrm{diag}([1]_q,[-1]_q)=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1)$; the specialization of $x$ is $\mathrm{diag}(1,-1)$, a nonzero operator, while the substitution $q=1$ into $K$ yields the identity. Hence the operator induced by $x$ is not obtained by substituting $q=1$ into the expression for $x$.

Step 3 (further witnesses). $[m]_q=(q^m-q^{-m})/(q-q^{-1})$: numerator and denominator vanish at $q=1$, while the correct specialization is the polynomial value $m$ ([[lem-q-one-toral-specialization-identifies-the-classical-cartan-generators]](ii)); the divided-power coefficient $\frac{1}{q^b-q^{-b}}\sum_{s=0}^{b-1}(q^{-2s}K-q^{2s}K^{-1})$ vanishes in numerator and denominator at $q=1$ yet acts on a weight vector $w$ of weight $\mu$ with $E_iw=0$ by the finite value $[\mu(h_i)-b+1]_i\mapsto\mu(h_i)-b+1$, as the string formula $E_iF_i^{(b)}w=[\mu(h_i)-b+1]_iF_i^{(b-1)}w$ shows by the geometric-sum identity. Each of these is an element of $U_A$ whose value at $q=1$ is defined through the integral form, not through term-by-term substitution.

Step 4 (correct statement). By [[prop-specialization-at-q-one-recovers-the-classical-enveloping-relations]], the specialization is the base change $U_A\otimes_Ak$ with $q\mapsto1$, which is well defined because the generators of $U_A$ are actual elements (and the operator matrices on lattice modules are polynomial); the cancellations in Steps 1-3 are handled inside $U_A$. No choice is used.
